hints: Notice this question mixes two different trends, one for the hydrides like $\text{HCl}$ to $\text{HI}$, and one for the elements $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$.
Recall what happens to the H-X bond as the halogen atom gets bigger, it gets longer and weaker, so think how that affects thermal stability and reducing power.
Connect bigger molecules with more electrons to stronger London forces and higher boiling points, then decide what that means for volatility.
walkthrough:
**Separate the Two Trends**

Think like a teacher and split the options. A and B are about hydrides, $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$, $\text{HI}$. C and D are about the elements, $\text{Cl}_2$, $\text{Br}_2$, $\text{I}_2$. We test each one separately.

**Check the Hydrides: Stability and Reducing Power**

Going down from Cl to I, the halogen atom gets larger. The H-X bond gets longer and weaker, so bond enthalpy falls.

$$\text{H-Cl} > \text{H-Br} > \text{H-I in bond strength}$$
That means the hydrides become less thermally stable and decompose more easily. A weaker bond also means the hydride is more easily oxidised, so it is a stronger reducing agent, with $\text{HI}$ strongest.

**Check the Elements: Forces and Volatility**

Going down from $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$, molecules get larger with many more electrons. Larger electron clouds are more easily polarised, so instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (van der Waals / London) forces increase.

$$\text{larger molecule} \rightarrow \text{stronger London forces} \rightarrow \text{higher mp/bp} \rightarrow \text{lower volatility}$$
This matches what we see: $\text{Cl}_2$ gas, $\text{Br}_2$ liquid, $\text{I}_2$ solid. So volatility decreases as forces increase.

options.A: Half right, half wrong. Hydrides do become less thermally stable down the group, but they become stronger reducing agents, not weaker. Students often mix this up, but weaker H-I bond means $\text{HI}$ gives up electrons more easily.
options.B: Incorrect on stability. Although halogen reactivity does decrease down the group, the hydrides become less thermally stable, not more, because the H-X bond gets weaker from $\text{HCl}$ to $\text{HI}$.
options.C: Correct and well linked. From $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$ the number of electrons and molecular size increase, so London (van der Waals) forces increase. Stronger forces mean more energy to separate molecules, so boiling points rise and volatility falls.
options.D: States the opposite of the true trend. Larger molecules have stronger, not weaker, intermolecular forces, so volatility decreases, not increases. This is a common trap if you confuse larger size with easier escape to gas.
